data.drivers#Drivers:
The 15 filesystem drivers available today (plus oci, a read-only image-as-filesystem overlay, and detect, a type-probing dispatch registry — both listed separately below since neither targets an on-disk format in the same sense as the rows in this table).
Module Read Write Format Label Symlinks Quota Snapshots Encryption On-disk format Platform apfs ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✅ — ✅ ✅ Real APFS on-disk (kext-mountable), GPT-aware macOS / iOS btrfs ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✕ ✕ — Single-device, CRC32c (btrfs-progs ≥ 5.x) Linux exfat ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✕ — — — exFAT Windows / removable ext4 ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✕ — ✕ ext4 — extents, 64-bit, flex_bg, dir htree, metadata_csum (CRC32c) Linux fat32 ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✕ — — — FAT32 cross-platform ffs ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✅ ✕ ✕ — NetBSD/OpenBSD FFSv1/FFSv2 — thin re-export of ufs BSD hfsplus ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ — — — HFS+ / HFSX (Mac OS Extended), big-endian catalog + extents-overflow B-trees macOS (legacy) iso9660 ✅ ✕ ✕ — ✅ — — — ISO 9660 / ECMA-119 + Rock Ridge (names/perms/symlinks) + Joliet (UCS-2 names) cross-platform (optical) ntfs ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✕ — — — Minimal in-image blob model — NOT the real NTFS on-disk format; a separate read-only reader parses genuine NTFS Windows squashfs ✅ ✕ ✅ — ✅ — — — SquashFS 4.0 read-only archive; gzip/xz/zstd/lzo/lz4 blocks + fragments Linux uefi ✅ ✅ ✅ — — — — — OVMF/EDK2 NvVar variable store; time-based authenticated writes firmware (UEFI) ufs ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✅ ✕ ✕ — UFS2 (FreeBSD 14.x) read+write; UFS1 read; NetBSD/OpenBSD FFSv1/FFSv2 (via ffs alias module) BSD xfs ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✕ XFS v5 (CRC32c, ftype) Linux zfs ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✅ ✕ ✅ ✅ read-only Single pool, single-vdev writer (multi-vdev/RAID-Z read-only) illumos / BSD / Linux oci ✅ ✕ — — ✅ — — — OCI/Docker image layers merged read-only (whiteouts, opaque dirs, hardlinks) any (image, not disk) Legend: ✅ supported by the driver · ✕ not yet implemented (the format has the feature) · — not applicable. Read = open & inspect · Write = mutate in place · Format = create a fresh image. Quota / Snapshots / Encryption reflect driver support, not just the on-disk format’s capability.
Also in the org: detect, a blkid-style type prober and driver-opener registry that dispatches to the drivers above — it isn’t an on-disk format itself, so it has no row.

data.apfs#apfs:
Apple File System.
Implements filesystem.Filesystem. No cgo, no root.
data.install#Install: go get github.com/go-filesystems/apfs Source: https://github.com/go-filesystems/apfs API reference: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-filesystems/apfs See the module’s README for full, up-to-date details.
data.not-implemented#Not implemented: Snapshot creation gated behind an Apple-private entitlement Some encrypted-container fsck stages are Apple-private
data.status#Status: Read Write Format Label Symlinks On-disk format ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✅ Real APFS on-disk (kext-mountable), GPT-aware
data.supported#Supported: Real APFS read: FS-tree traversal, multi-extent files, xattrs, sealed volumes Snapshot read (OpenSnapshot) Write & format kext-mountable containers FileVault software encryption (FormatContainerEncrypted) GPT + Apple DMG output POSIX special files Container resize (Resize)

data.ffs#ffs:
NetBSD/OpenBSD Berkeley Fast File System (FFS) — a thin re-export of ufs, since FFSv1/FFSv2 are the same on-disk format as UFS1/UFS2.
Implements filesystem.Filesystem. No cgo, no root.
data.install#Install: go get github.com/go-filesystems/ffs Source: https://github.com/go-filesystems/ffs API reference: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/go-filesystems/ffs See ufs and the module’s README for full, up-to-date details.
data.status#Status: Read Write Format Label Symlinks On-disk format ✅ ✅ ✅ — ✅ NetBSD/OpenBSD FFSv1/FFSv2 (= UFS1/UFS2), via the ufs driver
data.supported#Supported: Everything the ufs driver provides, under an import path that matches how NetBSD/OpenBSD callers think of the format (ffs.OpenFile, ffs.Open, ffs.OpenRW — thin aliases of the ufs entry points).

ISO 9660 / ECMA-119 optical-disc filesystem (.iso images), with Rock Ridge.
Implements filesystem.Filesystem. No cgo, no root.
data.not-implemented#Not implemented: Write/format — ISO 9660 is a read-only format; mutators return ErrReadOnly Rock Ridge deep-directory relocation (CL/PL/RE) Multi-extent files
data.status#Status: Read Write Format Label Symlinks On-disk format ✅ ✕ ✕ — ✅ ISO 9660 / ECMA-119 + Rock Ridge (names/perms/symlinks) + Joliet (UCS-2 names)
data.supported#Supported: Primary Volume Descriptor scan (CD001), logical block size, root record Directory-record parsing + per-sector padding-aware directory walk Contiguous single-extent file reads (multi-sector) Rock Ridge (SP/NM/PX/SL): real case-preserved long names, POSIX modes, symlink targets (ReadLink), and CE continuation areas Joliet (UCS-2 long names via the supplementary volume descriptor), used when Rock Ridge is absent Path resolution by real (Rock Ridge / Joliet) name, with a case-insensitive fallback for base ISO names

data.ntfs#ntfs:
Windows NT filesystem.
Implements filesystem.Filesystem. No cgo, no root.
Lightweight, test-oriented. Use a real NTFS implementation for on-disk compatibility.
data.status#Status: Read Write Format Label Symlinks On-disk format ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✕ Minimal in-image blob model — NOT the real NTFS on-disk format
data.supported#Supported: Read/write files (blob storage inside the image) Directories, recursive delete, rename In-image free-list reuse In-image Grow / Shrink / Resize and compaction (Compact, FragmentationStats, Layout) A separate read-only reader parses genuine on-disk NTFS: LZNT1 decompression, named streams (ADS), $REPARSE_POINT symlinks/junctions, $ATTRIBUTE_LIST, volume label

data.interface#Interface:
Every driver implements the contract defined in go-filesystems/interface (package filesystem):
type Filesystem interface { Close() error ReadFile(path string) ([]byte, error) ListDir(path string) ([]DirEntry, error) Stat(path string) (Stat, error) WriteFile(path string, data []byte, perm os.FileMode) error ReadLink(path string) (string, error) MkDir(path string, perm os.FileMode) error DeleteFile(path string) error DeleteDir(path string) error Rename(oldPath, newPath string) error } Optional capabilities are probed via type assertion:
Labeller — volume label get/set. Resizer — grow/shrink (returns ErrShrinkUnsupported where shrink is impossible). See the package reference for the full API, including DirEntry and Stat.

data.changes#Changing the image: In the explorer you can upload, make folders, rename, copy and delete, on fat32, exfat and ext4. The other drivers refuse writes. The file you dropped is never written. A change lands in a copy-on-write layer under the drivers, in the tab’s memory (at most 256 MiB), and inside a LUKS container it lands encrypted. Download the modified image then saves the original with the changes in it, in the same format. Opening another image, or leaving, asks first while changes are not downloaded.
data.encrypted#Encrypted images:
A LUKS1 or LUKS2 container (go-fde/luks) is recognised by its header, and the page asks for its password. The engine unlocks it and opens the filesystem in the payload: detected, or the one chosen in the list. The facts then read e.g. ext4 in LUKS. A wrong password is refused, and the form stays to try again.
APFS FileVault containers are not supported yet: go-filesystems/apfs cannot read one through its decrypted device so far, and that is being fixed there first.
data.explorer#Open in the explorer: Once an image is open, open in the explorer loads the go-fileshare explorer in a same-origin frame. It is fetched only then (4.1 MB compressed), and browses the image the way it browses a fileshare server, over WebDAV. None of its requests reach a network. The page hands each one to the engine, which answers it with go-filesystems/webdav over the open image. Closing the explorer unloads it.
data.how-it-works#How it works: The Go engine runs in a Web Worker. Its io.ReaderAt reads the dropped file with FileReaderSync.readAsArrayBuffer(file.slice(off, end)) — a synchronous read that the File API allows only in workers — so the drivers’ synchronous reads never block the page, and the image is never loaded whole. A block cache (64 KiB blocks, LRU, 16 MiB) turns a driver’s many small metadata reads into a few block reads; file contents bypass it. A checkbox on the page turns it off for comparison. The page is plain HTML, CSS and a few KiB of JavaScript, talking to the worker with three coarse requests: open, list a directory, read part of a file.
data.playground#Playground:
https://go-filesystems.github.io/playground/ — open a disk image in your browser. The page says which filesystem it is, lets you browse the tree, view small files and download any file. Everything runs in WebAssembly in your browser: nothing is uploaded.
No image at hand? Make a sample FAT32 image: the page formats one in memory with fat32.FormatImage, writes a few files into it, opens it again through detect, and lets you download it.
data.safety#Safety:
The image is untrusted input: every answer is bounded (entries per listing, bytes per read), a driver panic becomes an error, a request that takes more than 30 s restarts the engine, and names from the image are shown as text, never as HTML.
A LUKS header is untrusted too: it says how much key derivation unlocking costs. The engine refuses a header that asks for more than 2²² PBKDF2 iterations, or for Argon2 beyond 16 passes or 1 GiB, before deriving anything (go-fde/luks OpenFromLimited). An unlock gets 180 s.
The password goes to the engine in the tab for one open. It is not stored and never sent anywhere. The page empties the field, and the engine clears its copy once the container is unlocked or refused.
Source: https://github.com/go-filesystems/playground
data.what-it-opens#What it opens: Filesystem Found Viewing and downloading fat32, exfat, ext4, iso9660, squashfs at offset 0, by detect streamed in 4 MiB pieces (filesystem.Opener) ntfs, hfsplus, ufs at offset 0, by detect read whole, files up to 64 MiB apfs, btrfs, xfs, zfs in a disk image’s GPT or MBR table, through a read-only block device read whole, files up to 64 MiB The Filesystem list chooses the driver. Detect it, the default, asks detect; when nothing opens at offset 0, the four disk-image drivers are tried in turn. Choosing a filesystem forces that driver, for an image detect gets wrong or cannot recognise.
